facts.query: How big is Earth compared with its biggest features?
facts.explanation: A person, the largest tree, the highest mountain and one of the great canyons all look tiny next to the planet itself. Even Mount Everest is a barely visible bump on a globe: Earth's surface is remarkably smooth for its size.

facts.query: What were the biggest volcanic eruptions in history?
facts.explanation: A handful of eruptions changed history: they buried cities, cooled the global climate and caused famines far from the volcano. Tambora was the largest eruption in recorded history, and its ash led to the 'Year Without a Summer' that followed.

facts.label: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
facts.description: Mount Vesuvius erupts and buries the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program

facts.label: Laki fissure eruption
facts.description: Iceland's Laki fissure begins an eight-month eruption; its toxic gases cause crop failure and famine.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program

facts.label: Tambora
facts.description: Mount Tambora, Indonesia, reaches its climax: the largest eruption in recorded history.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program

facts.label: Krakatau
facts.description: Krakatau's explosions are heard thousands of kilometres away and trigger deadly tsunamis.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program

facts.label: Novarupta
facts.description: Alaska's Novarupta produces the largest eruption of the 20th century.
facts.sourceNote: USGS Alaska Volcano Observatory

facts.label: Mount St. Helens
facts.description: A landslide uncorks Mount St. Helens in Washington State in a huge lateral blast.
facts.sourceNote: USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory

facts.label: Pinatubo
facts.description: Pinatubo, Philippines, injects so much sulfur into the stratosphere that global temperatures dip for about two years.
facts.sourceNote: USGS / PHIVOLCS

facts.label: Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai
facts.description: An undersea volcano in Tonga sends a plume into the mesosphere and a pressure wave around the globe.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program

facts.query: If Earth's history were squeezed into one day, when did life appear?
facts.explanation: Squeeze Earth's whole history into a single day and most of it belongs to microbes. Animals with skeletons arrive only in the late evening, dinosaurs vanish shortly before midnight, and our own species shows up in the final seconds.

facts.label: Earth forms
facts.description: Earth forms from the disk of gas and dust around the young Sun.
facts.sourceNote: USGS, age of the Earth (4.54 ± 0.05 billion years)

facts.label: Oldest known minerals
facts.description: Zircon crystals from Jack Hills, Australia, show that a solid crust and liquid water existed.
facts.sourceNote: Wilde et al., Nature 2001 (Jack Hills zircons)

facts.label: Oldest widely accepted fossils
facts.description: Microbial mats leave stromatolites in Western Australia's Pilbara region.
facts.sourceNote: Geological Survey of Western Australia / Smithsonian NMNH (Dresser Formation)

facts.label: Great Oxidation Event
facts.description: Photosynthesizing microbes start filling the atmosphere with oxygen.
facts.sourceNote: NASA Astrobiology / peer-reviewed estimates (about 2.4 billion years ago)

facts.label: Cambrian explosion begins
facts.description: Animals with shells and skeletons diversify rapidly at the start of the Cambrian Period.
facts.sourceNote: International Commission on Stratigraphy, Geologic Time Scale (base of the Cambrian)

facts.label: First land plants
facts.description: Simple plants related to liverworts begin to colonize land.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian NMNH, fossil spore evidence (about 470 million years ago)

facts.label: First dinosaurs
facts.description: The earliest known dinosaurs appear in the Late Triassic.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian NMNH, Late Triassic fossils (about 233 million years ago)

facts.label: Dinosaurs wiped out
facts.description: An asteroid impact at Chicxulub ends the age of non-avian dinosaurs.
facts.sourceNote: International Commission on Stratigraphy, Geologic Time Scale (end of the Cretaceous)

facts.label: Homo sapiens appears
facts.description: The oldest known fossils of our species, from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco.
facts.sourceNote: Hublin et al., Nature 2017; Smithsonian Human Origins

facts.label: Last ice age ends
facts.description: The Holocene epoch begins as the last glacial period ends.
facts.sourceNote: International Commission on Stratigraphy, Geologic Time Scale (base of the Holocene, 11,700 years before 2000)

plan.title: Earth's history on a clock
plan.caption: Earth forms at midnight; the present is the next midnight.

facts.query: What is the air made of?
facts.explanation: Dry air is mostly nitrogen, with oxygen a distant second and argon a small third. Carbon dioxide is only a trace gas, yet it has a large effect on climate, and its share keeps rising.

facts.query: How much of Earth is covered by ocean, forest and ice?
facts.explanation: Ocean covers most of Earth's surface. On land, forests cover close to a third of the area, while glaciers and ice sheets, mostly in Antarctica and Greenland, cover about a tenth.

facts.query: How many Eiffel Towers would it take to reach the bottom of the Mariana Trench?
facts.explanation: The Challenger Deep, at the southern end of the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific, is the deepest known point in the ocean. Stacking Eiffel Towers tip to base, it would take a whole column of them to reach the seafloor from the surface.
